reason: The sources provide a clear narrative of professional jealousy and ignored warnings leading to a catastrophic and preventable loss of life.
story: In 1900, Galveston was the 'Jewel of Texas,' a booming metropolis of Victorian mansions. Local weather chief Isaac Cline had publicly declared it 'impossible' for a major hurricane to strike the low-lying island. This complacency proved fatal. While world-class Jesuit meteorologists in Cuba tracked a monster heading for Texas, US Weather Bureau director Willis Moore blocked their reports out of professional jealousy and banned the word 'hurricane' to avoid 'panic.' On September 8, the Category 4 storm struck an unprepared city. A 15-foot surge swallowed the island, which peaked at only 8.7 feet in elevation. Survivors described a 'wall of debris' crushing everything in its path. At an orphanage, nuns tied children to their waists with clotheslines; they were found the next day, still tethered and drowned. With 8,000 dead, survivors were forced to burn bodies in massive beach pyres. Galveston survived, but its golden era was swept away forever.
angle: The deadliest natural disaster in US history was caused by a US Weather Bureau director who blocked life-saving warnings from Cuban experts because of professional jealousy.

claims.claim: The 1900 Galveston hurricane is the deadliest natural disaster in United States history.
The storm's death toll is most commonly cited as 8,000 people, though estimates range from 6,000 to 12,000.
In 1891, Isaac Cline wrote that it was impossible for a hurricane of significant strength to strike Galveston.
The highest natural point on Galveston Island was only 8.7 feet above sea level.
Weather Bureau director Willis Moore blocked telegraph reports from advanced Cuban meteorologists due to post-war tensions.
The Weather Bureau banned the use of words like 'hurricane' or 'cyclone' to avoid panicking the public.
Cuban forecasters correctly predicted the storm would move toward Texas, while US forecasters predicted it would hit Florida and the East Coast.
The hurricane made landfall as a Category 4 storm with sustained winds of approximately 145 mph.
A 15-foot storm surge completely inundated the island, which was already being flooded by early morning.
At St. Mary's Orphanage, ten nuns tied 90 children to themselves with clotheslines; nearly all of them drowned.
Flying debris, including slate shingles and bricks, became airborne projectiles that killed many survivors.
Thousands of bodies were initially loaded onto barges and dumped at sea, but they washed back onto the beaches.
Because burial was impossible, funeral pyres were used to burn the dead day and night for weeks after the storm.
Isaac Cline's own house collapsed during the storm, killing his pregnant wife, Cora.
To protect against future storms, the city began an engineering project to raise its grade by up to 17 feet.
The disaster ended Galveston's 'Golden Era' as investors shifted their focus to Houston.
Men were forcibly recruited at gunpoint or bayonet point to collect and dispose of the dead.
High pressure over the Florida Keys pushed the storm toward Texas, preventing the recurve predicted by US forecasters.
The storm surge destroyed about 7,000 buildings in Galveston, including more than 3,600 homes.
No ship-to-shore wireless communication was available in 1900 to track the strengthening storm.

disputed: Isaac Cline's heroic beach patrol: According to his own accounts, he warned thousands of people, but some historians find no survivor corroboration and argue his earlier dismissal of a seawall caused the high death toll.
Exact death toll: Sources cite ranges between 6,000 and 12,000; the script should note that 8,000 is the most commonly accepted official figure.
